finding.headline: At 49 and 50, the household can focus on the 401(k) limit and the Medicare rule at 65.
details: For 2027, the 401(k) limit is $25,500. Once you reach age 50, the catch-up limit is $8,500, so you can contribute up to $34,000 a year in most 401(k) plans.
Ages 60 to 63 have a higher catch-up limit of $11,750 in 2027. Keep this in mind for the years before retirement.
Sign up for Medicare at age 65, even if you delay Social Security. If you do not, your Medicare coverage may be delayed and cost more.

finding.headline: About 20% of your income goes to tax now, and about 10% of withdrawals in retirement.
details: Right now, total tax is $40,868 a year on $205,000 of pay. Your savings are 86% in pre-tax accounts like a 401(k), so most withdrawals will be taxed.
The plan draws on taxable savings first, then pre-tax accounts, and Roth accounts last. You have no Roth savings yet, so that last step does not apply today.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Please check the order with a tax professional before you act.

finding.headline: You can count on $67,700 a year: $39,900 for basics and $27,800 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $39,900 a year.
Your spending goal of $85,000 a year lasts in 24 of 100 scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.

Until you retire you save about $30,231 a year: $14,000 into a 401(k) or IRA, $3,300 from your employer's match, $12,931 of take-home pay left after your spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Your spending in retirement leaves out the mortgage. The payments left after you retire, until 2047, are counted as a cost of their own.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $68,000 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 69 for each of you, which pays about $78,900 a year.
A partner with little pay of their own gets half of the other's benefit at 67, less if started sooner.
After the first death (at the shorter life expectancy), Social Security falls to the larger of your two benefits, about $40,700 a year, and spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay and the child tax credit applies. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 97. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
